source_spans.locator: Science 269, published p.1880, Abstract and opening paragraphs: arm-state estimation in the dark; distinction between dynamics prediction from current state plus motor command and other estimation routes

Science 269, published p.1880, experiment/results paragraph and Figure 1: null, assistive, and resistive force conditions; movement-duration dependence of localization bias and variance; force changes bias but not variance

Science 269, published pp.1880-1881, observer-model description and Figure 2A: current state estimate plus motor command predicts next state; predicted and actual sensory feedback form an error; recursively updated gain weights the sensory correction

Science 269, published p.1881, Figure 2B-E and accompanying text: simulated bias/variance patterns, force-dependent bias effects, and time-dependent shift from dynamics prediction toward sensory correction

Science 269, published p.1882, concluding interpretation and note 13: combined prediction-plus-correction model reproduces the observed pattern; motor-outflow-only and sensory-inflow-only alternatives fail in distinct ways; further lesion/afference predictions are prospective

Science 269, published p.1882, Methods/note 8: eight untrained male participants, 300 trials each, 2-s visual calibration, dark movement until a tone, randomly selected null/assistive/resistive 3-N force field, and terminal visual thumb-location report

Science 269, published p.1882, model equations/parameter note: process and sensory noise are explicit; the recursive estimator is an optimal linear estimator under the model; several fit parameters were chosen by trial and error for qualitative capture

conditions: arm movements are made without visual feedback after an initial visual calibration period
each movement occurs in a randomly selected null, constant assistive, or constant resistive 3-N force field
the recursive estimator includes process noise and sensory-output noise and is linear under the stated model
the empirical model comparison is qualitative; several simulation parameters were selected by trial and error to capture the observed data pattern
population: eight untrained male participants, 300 trials each
task: move the unseen right hand left or right until an auditory stop cue and then report the unseen thumb location visually with a trackball
temporal_scope: the arm is viewed for 2 s before darkness; movement duration varies across trials; each trial yields a terminal localization report, and temporal propagation is reconstructed across trials of different durations
the model recursively updates the state estimate during movement, with relative weighting shifting from dynamics-based prediction toward sensory correction over approximately the first second

relations.description: the dynamics-based process predicts the next arm state from the current estimated state and the motor command
the current estimated arm state is transformed into an expected sensory output
the sensory discrepancy is the difference between actual reafferent feedback and predicted feedback
the updated state estimate combines the dynamics-based prediction with a gain-weighted sensory correction
as movement proceeds after the initial visual calibration, relative weighting shifts from the dynamics-based prediction toward sensory correction and then becomes approximately stable
the terminal visual report provides the observable localization error used to probe the otherwise latent arm-state estimate
errors accumulated across trials are summarized into signed bias and variance as functions of movement duration and force condition
localization bias first rises to an overestimation peak near 1 s and then declines gradually with longer movement duration
localization variance rises during approximately the first second of movement and then approaches a plateau
assistive force increases localization bias whereas resistive force decreases it relative to the null condition
variance changes with movement duration, while the source reports no significant differential variance propagation between assistive and resistive force conditions
the recursive prediction-plus-correction model qualitatively reproduces the observed biphasic bias, variance plateau, and differential force effect
the motor-outflow-only alternative predicts monotonically increasing bias and variance rather than the observed temporal pattern
the sensory-inflow-only alternative cannot reproduce the differential effect of external forces on localization bias
